title: Git Tags, Versioning and Patch Transfer: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on lightweight vs annotated tags, pushing tags, semantic versioning and git describe, then cherry-pick (conflicts and -x for backports) and moving commits with format-patch and git am.

chapters.title: Tags: Lightweight vs Annotated
points: A tag is a fixed, human-readable name for one commit; unlike a branch it never moves as you commit
Lightweight tag: `git tag v1.0` is just a ref pointing straight at a commit, with no extra metadata
Annotated tag: `git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release 1.0"` creates a tag object storing tagger, date, message and an optional GPG signature
Comparison: annotated tags carry metadata and show in `git show`; lightweight tags are bookmarks. Use annotated for releases, lightweight for private temporary marks
Mistake: relying on lightweight tags for releases, since `git describe` ignores them by default and they hold no author or date

chapters.title: Pushing and Managing Tags
points: `git push` does not send tags; push one with `git push origin v1.0`
Push all tags with `git push origin --tags`, or only annotated tags reachable from pushed commits with `git push --follow-tags`
Tag an older commit with `git tag -a v0.9 <sha> -m "msg"`; list with `git tag -l 'v1.*'`; inspect with `git show v1.0`
Delete a tag locally with `git tag -d v1.0` and on the remote with `git push origin --delete v1.0` (or `git push origin :refs/tags/v1.0`)
Mistake: moving a published tag with `git tag -f` and force-pushing; other clones keep the old tag, so cut a new version instead

chapters.title: Semantic Versioning and git describe
points: SemVer format is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes
Bumping resets lower numbers to zero (1.4.2 + feature = 1.5.0; 1.5.0 + breaking = 2.0.0); pre-release looks like 1.0.0-rc.1 and sorts before 1.0.0
`git describe` prints the nearest reachable annotated tag, e.g. `v1.2.0-5-g3f9a1c2`: 5 commits after v1.2.0, with the abbreviated hash prefixed by `g`
Flags: `--tags` includes lightweight tags, `--always` falls back to the commit hash, `--dirty` appends `-dirty` for uncommitted changes, `--abbrev=0` prints only the tag name
Mistake: `git describe` fails with `No names found` when no annotated tag is reachable; also, an exact tag match prints just the tag name

chapters.title: Cherry-Pick and Its Conflicts
points: `git cherry-pick <sha>` copies the changes of one commit onto the current branch as a new commit with a new hash
Ranges: `git cherry-pick A B C` for several commits, `A^..C` for an inclusive range, and `-n` to apply changes without committing
It replays the commit's diff as a three-way merge, so it can conflict when the target branch differs in the same lines
Resolve a conflict by editing the files, `git add`, then `git cherry-pick --continue`; abandon with `--abort`, or skip one commit with `--skip`
Mistake: picking a commit that depends on earlier unpicked commits, or picking then later merging the source branch; the duplicate commit can cause confusing conflicts

chapters.title: Backports with cherry-pick -x
points: Backport: apply a fix from main to a maintained release branch, e.g. `git switch release-1.2` then `git cherry-pick -x <sha>`
`-x` appends the line `(cherry picked from commit <sha>)` to the new commit message, recording the origin
Use `-x` only for picks between public branches; the sha reference helps trace and audit, and it is not added by default
Comparison: cherry-pick copies one commit; merge brings the whole history. Backport only the fix, not unrelated features
Mistake: cherry-picking a merge commit without `-m 1` fails; `-m` selects which parent is the mainline

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Tags and Patch Transfer
points: Tags: `git tag v1`, `git tag -a v1 -m msg`, `git push origin v1`, `git push --follow-tags`, `git tag -d v1`
Describe: `git describe --tags --always --dirty`, output format `tag-N-gHASH`
Cherry-pick: `git cherry-pick -x <sha>`, then `--continue`, `--abort`, `--skip` for conflicts
Patches: `git format-patch -3` or `git format-patch main..HEAD` creates one .patch file per commit; `-o dir` sets the output folder
Apply: `git am *.patch` keeps author, date and message; on conflict fix, `git add`, then `git am --continue` (or `--abort`); `git apply` changes files only with no commit
